A pelicanry is a place where pelicans gather specifically to breed — to court, mate, nest, lay eggs, and raise their young.
What exactly does "breeding place" mean here?

Pelicans are colonial birds, meaning they don't breed alone in isolation. Instead, large numbers of them instinctively return, season after season, to the same specific location to go through their entire breeding cycle together. That special location — the site where all of this happens as a group — is the pelicanry.

At a pelicanry, you'd see:

  • Pelicans selecting nesting spots and building nests
  • Pairs courting each other
  • Eggs being laid and incubated
  • Chicks being hatched and fed
  • Young pelicans gradually growing until they can survive on their own

It is not just any place where pelicans happen to gather or feed. It is specifically and exclusively the site tied to their breeding activity.
Is it a natural place or a man-made one?

It can be either. A pelicanry can be a completely wild, natural site — such as a remote island, a sheltered coastal area, or an inland wetland — that pelicans have chosen for generations. It can also be a managed or protected site, maintained by humans (such as a wildlife sanctuary or zoo), specifically to house pelicans and allow them to breed in a safe environment.
How does it compare to similar words?

English has several words of the same type that describe breeding or dwelling places of specific birds or animals. Understanding this pattern will make "pelicanry" stick better:

  • A rookery is a breeding colony of rooks (a type of crow), or by extension, a colony of other birds like penguins, or even seals.
  • A heronry is a place where herons nest and breed in a group.
  • A swannery is a place — often a managed one — where swans live and breed.
  • A pelicanry, naturally, is the same thing but for pelicans.

All of these words share the same underlying idea: a dedicated location tied to a specific species' breeding life.

No. "Pelicanry" is a genuinely rare word. You will almost never encounter it in everyday conversation or general reading. It belongs to the specialized vocabulary of ornithology (the study of birds), wildlife management, and nature writing. It appears in Merriam-Webster's Unabridged Dictionary, which is a mark of its legitimacy, but it is not the kind of word you'd find in a standard dictionary aimed at everyday users. If you ever come across it, it will almost certainly be in a formal nature documentary, a scientific text about bird colonies, or a historical account of wildlife habitats.
A simple sentence to lock it in
Think of it this way: just as a brewery is a place built around the making of beer, a pelicanry is a place built around (or naturally used for) the making of new pelicans — their breeding site.
